stories.title: US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll quits amid Iran war
stories.summary: US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has resigned amid ongoing war with Iran, following clashes with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over Army modernisation, officer firings, and blocked promotions.

article_sentences: US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has resigned amid ongoing war with Iran, following clashes with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over Army modernisation, officer firings, and blocked promotions.

New York: In the midst of the lingering war with Iran, US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has dramatically resigned over simmering differences with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, according to media reports.
Driscoll handed in his resignation after a meeting with President Donald Trump on Monday, local media reported, quoting officials.
White House has not confirmed the resignation.
He had clashed with Hegseth over the Army’s modernisation, the firings of several key officers and the blocking of promotions of others.
Driscoll is the second senior civilian military official to leave during the Iran War; Navy Secretary John Phelan was fired in April.
Under the US military hierarchy, the Navy, Army and Air Force have separate secretaries under the Defence Secretary.
In the midst of a six-month confrontation with Iran, the Army is without both its civilian head as well as a permanent military chief after the firing of Army Chief of Staff General Randy George.

Army Vice Chief of Staff General James Mingus was fired last October, and General Christopher LaNeve, who was nominated to succeed him, has not received the Senate’s approval — a requisite for senior military appointments.

Like Trump, Hegseth said the Iran war would be over in weeks but is leading a military virtually stuck in the conflict, and he has fired three other generals who could have been successors to George, creating a vacuum.
While troops have not entered a ground war with Iran, they provide crucial defence against Iranian missiles and drones, and some soldiers have died in attacks from Tehran on bases in the Gulf region.
Driscoll had himself seen combat in Iraq as an Army Lieutenant and was seen as a possible successor to Hegseth, who has not been able to lead the military to the promised quick victory.

The External Affairs Ministry said the two leaders discussed conflicts in West Asia and in the Black Sea region, where, in recent months, Indian seafarers have been attacked by both Russian and Ukrainian forces.

stories.headline: Move from 'endless war towards end of war': PM Modi tells Russian President Putin
stories.title: Move from 'endless war towards end of war': PM Modi tells Russian President Putin
stories.summary: Bishkek, Sep 01: Calling for an immediate end to the Russia-Ukraine conflict, Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to move from "endless war towards end of war”, asserting that a peaceful resolution of the conflict is humanity's shared priority. In a meeting with Putin on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in this capital city of Kyrgyzstan, Modi said every day of war sets the humanity back and that India, the land of Gandhi and Buddha, supports all efforts towards peace and will continue to do so. The two leaders also extensively deliberated on ongoing cooperation in areas of trade and investment and energy and fertiliser security among others. "We have always discussed the Ukraine issue. When we last met, you had extensively briefed me on all aspects of it. India supports all efforts for peace and will continue to do so," Modi said in his televised opening remarks at the meeting. "Every day spent on war pushes humanity backwards, whereas every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm. We must move from endless war towards the end of war, which is very crucial for the well-being of humanity," the prime minister said in Hindi. "A peaceful resolution of all issues as soon as possible is the call of humanity, and this is also India’s message. The land of Gandhi and Buddha has a single message: the path of peace," he said. Modi and Putin travelled together in the Russian President's limousine to Nomad Games. Television footage showed them jointly entering the venue for the inauguration ceremony of the games. The two leaders had travelled in the same car in the Chinese city of Tianjin during the SCO summit last year too. The talks between the two leaders came over a week before Putin travels to India to attend the annual BRICS summit. The prime minister also made a mention of the Russian President's visit to New Delhi last year. "Your visit to India last year was highly successful and truly memorable. It is a matter of deep satisfaction for us that our cooperation continues to scale new heights and that we are working together for the welfare of the people of both nations," Modi said. "Focusing on national interest as the paramount priority has been our shared approach, and this will remain our guiding principle in the future as well." Putin, on his part, said Russia-India relations have witnessed an upswing on the basis of the special and privileged partnership. At a media briefing, Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri said there was a discussion between the two leaders on trade with a focus on increasing Indian exports to Russia in several areas. The foreign secretary also noted that there has been significant progress in addressing issues like non-tariff barriers and market access for Indian products in Russia since the last meeting between the two leaders. Misri also said that Modi and Putin discussed the Ukraine issue and the prime minister emphasised the importance India attaches to dialogue and diplomacy to resolve it. Modi emphasised on the need to "move from endless war to the end of war", he said. The prime minister also reiterated India's readiness to do whatever is feasible and necessary at its end the conflict as it is exacting a very heavy toll on the global community at large, the foreign secretary said. The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said Modi and Putin reviewed progress in bilateral cooperation in a range of fields, including political, economic, defence, energy, space, mobility and people-to-people ties. The two leaders welcomed the outcome of the 27th India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic and Cultural matters, held on August 24 in Moscow, it said. Modi and Putin exchanged views on India-Russia engagement in the multilateral arena, in particular in BRICS and also shared perspectives on key regional and global issues of mutual interest, including the conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region which have impacted maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers, the MEA said. The prime minister reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy were the way forward in resolving conflicts, it said in a statement. "The two leaders agreed to remain engaged to further strengthen the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between the two countries, which continues to register significant growth and has shown resilience in the backdrop of geopolitical uncertainties," it said. "The prime minister stated that he looks forward to welcoming President Putin in India for the 18th BRICS Summit on September 12 and 13," it added. At the media briefing, Misri also responded to a question on the issue of several Indians serving in the Russian military. "The issue of our nationals being recruited into the Russian armed forces has been discussed between India and Russia at various levels on various occasions," he said. "Our embassy in Moscow is monitoring this situation regularly with regard to the release and repatriation of these Indian citizens. We are in discussions with the Russian side to ensure that any cases that remain are discharged at the earliest," he added. "At last count, we had information about 227 Indian nationals who had been recruited into the Russian army. And out of that number, we have information that 139 of our nationals have been discharged from the army. Unfortunately, we also have information about 51 people who have perished so far," he said. "This remains an issue on which we are in constant discussions with the Russian side."

stories.headline: Nepal floods triggered by massive ice-rock fall, not earthquake or GLOF: experts
stories.title: Nepal floods triggered by massive ice-rock fall, not earthquake or GLOF: experts
stories.summary: The devastating floods that swept through Nepal were triggered by a massive fall of ice and rock in the high Himalayas and not by an earthquake or glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF), according to experts. The flash floods that triggered near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26 swept through the Bhotekoshi River corridor, destroying homes, roads and bridges and damaging hydropower projects. The death toll from the disaster crossed 900 on Monday, while over 4000 people remained missing, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. A study, commissioned by the Nepal Environment Society (NES), found that a huge mass of ice, rock and debris fell from around 5,200 metres in the Langtang Lirung area of Rasuwa and entered the Lhende River, generating a powerful debris-laden flood that travelled downstream through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers. Bishal Nath Upreti, president of the Nepal Centre for Disaster Management, said initial theories that the disaster was caused by a GLOF or an earthquake had subsequently been discarded. “Initially, many thought it was a glacial lake outburst flood, or GLOF. Later, it became clear that there had been no lake burst in Tibet along that line, so that theory was discarded,” Upreti told PTI Videos. It was then thought that an earthquake had triggered the ice and rock fall, but the US Geological Survey later clarified that the sequence was the other way around, he said. “A massive rock and ice fall into the valley generated the earthquake,” Upreti said, adding that the earthquake was initially recorded at magnitude 4.2 and later revised to 5.2. “So, the disaster was not caused by an earthquake; rather, the falling ice and rock generated the earthquake,” he said. The NES study, released on Sunday, also concluded that the disaster was not caused by a GLOF. Researchers from NES analysed satellite imagery, hydrological and meteorological data, terrain characteristics and changes in elevation and slope along the river system and found no evidence of a lake outburst. According to the study, the ice-rock mass began falling from the northern part of Langtang Lirung at around 8:37 am on Wednesday. It descended steep terrain from about 5,200 metres before reaching the Lhende River at around 2,930 metres. Satellite images showed major geographical changes across about 10 square kilometres, while a section of glacier covering approximately 0.56 square kilometres had broken away. Upreti said scientists were still trying to establish the precise mechanism behind the disaster as no one had yet reached the site and much of the research was based on satellite imagery. “One emerging hypothesis is that it was actually a massive rockslide, with the ice riding over the falling rock, rather than the glacier itself sliding down,” he said, cautioning that the theory could not yet be confirmed. The NES study found that the ice-rock mass travelled about 22 km to Rasuwagadhi in just over seven minutes, reaching an estimated average speed of 46.3 metres per second, or 167 kmph. Its speed fell to around 73 kmph between Rasuwagadhi and Betrabati and to about 22 kmph further downstream. Despite slowing, the flow continued carrying huge quantities of rock, sediment and soil, the report said. The study also found no evidence of exceptionally heavy rainfall in the upper watershed that day, weakening the assumption that the disaster was caused solely by extreme rainfall or a cloudburst. Upreti said a second, smaller flood occurred after another landslide around three hours and eight minutes later created a temporary dam that subsequently breached. “Fortunately, it flowed slowly and did not result in a major disaster,” he said. The floods also caused extensive damage to hydropower infrastructure. Citing preliminary Nepal Electricity Authority data, the NES report said 13 hydropower projects and one solar project were affected, taking around 431 MW of generation capacity out of the system. The study said further field investigation was needed to determine the precise geological mechanism, the contribution of melting ice and whether the river was temporarily blocked upstream.

stories.headline: Rethinking Himalayan Floods
stories.title: Rethinking Himalayan Floods
stories.summary: The flash floods that tore through the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26 were, for a few days, were described as a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF). That assumption turned out to be wrong. Satellite analysis later showed the disaster began not with a lake bursting its banks, but with a chunk of glacier, ice and rock giving way on an unstable slope and crashing into a river valley below. For years, the dominant framework for understanding Himalayan flood risk has been the glacial lake. The Nepal event is a reminder that a slope does not need a lake beneath it to become a disaster. Fractured bedrock and glacier ice sitting on a steep incline can fail on their own, and once that debris reaches a river channel, it can turn into a flood just as destructive as a GLOF. Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh have already been flagged as the most climate-sensitive part of the Himalayan range, warming faster than other sectors and facing much sharper temperature rises in the decades ahead. Kishtwar, Doda, Ramban and large parts of Ladakh sit in terrain that scientists say closely resembles the slopes that failed in Nepal. Kashmir’s own glacial lake studies have already flagged thousands of buildings and more than a dozen bridges within potential flood zones. What has not been done, by the scientists’ own account, is a comparable assessment of the unstable rock and ice slopes themselves. A disaster elsewhere prompts a round of statements and studies, some monitoring stations go up, and attention moves on before the harder work of mapping is finished. Permafrost and bedrock studies are slower and less visible, and there is no local memory of a slope collapse in the way there is of a lake breach. That should not be mistaken for safety. The scientists quoted after the Nepal disaster are asking for something more basic: that the slopes above Kashmir, Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh be studied with the same seriousness as the lakes below them, before one of them fails without warning. Given how much of the region’s population and infrastructure sits downstream, that is a reasonable ask, and one the government should not wait for the next disaster to act on.

article_sentences: Devastating floods near the border with China have killed at least 939 people in Nepal, while the number of missing in the country dropped to 3,925, its disaster authority said on Monday, 31 August, as rescue efforts entered a sixth day.

The Nepali Army has rescued 279 people from hydropower projects battered by last week’s Bhotekoshi floods, but hundreds of workers remain unaccounted for as rescuers scour damaged project sites, tunnels and river corridors for survivors.

The Independent Power Producers’ Association Nepal (IPPAN), an umbrella body representing private-sector power developers, said on Monday that the whereabouts of 894 people working at 11 hydropower projects along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river corridors remained unknown.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the Nepali Army had rescued 254 people from the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project and nine from the 5MW Mailung Khola Hydropower Project.
Search teams were continuing to probe the tunnels of Upper Trishuli-1, where Nepali, South Korean and Chinese personnel were working together in a race against time.
IPPAN said 573 people associated with the 216MW Upper Trishuli-1 project remained out of contact, underscoring the scale of the disaster that swept through Nepal’s mountainous hydropower belt.
At the 111MW Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project in Rasuwa, two people were rescued, but a search of the project’s tunnel found no others.
A joint team from the Nepali and Chinese armies entered the tunnel after fears that workers could have been trapped deep inside following the sudden rise of the Bhote Koshi River.
“The rescue team led by the Nepali Army has returned after searching the tunnel...
and finding no people inside,” the Prime Minister’s Secretariat said on Monday.
Rescue operations were also under way at the Langtang Khola and Chilime hydropower projects in Rasuwa.
Nepali Army personnel, an Indian rescue team and Nepali workers were attempting to clear tunnel entrances blocked by debris and flood damage.

stories.headline: Army reviews operational preparedness along LoC
stories.title: Army reviews operational preparedness along LoC
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 31: General Officer Commanding (GOC) White Knight Corps, Lieutenant General P K Mishra visited the Ace of Spades Division to review its operational preparedness and assess the evolving security dynamics, the Army said on Monday. During the visit, the Corps Commander was briefed on the division’s operational commitments, capability development, Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) and counter-UAS capabilities, besides the roadmap for enhancing operational effectiveness in the coming days. The Army said the visit focused on strengthening preparedness in view of the changing battlefield environment and emerging security challenges. The Corps Commander emphasised the need to further enhance operational effectiveness and exhorted all ranks to remain future-ready, agile and adaptable to emerging challenges. The White Knight Corps, which is responsible for the security of the Jammu region including areas along the Line of Control (LoC) has been regularly reviewing operational preparedness and surveillance capabilities amid evolving security dynamics. In a post on X, the White Knight Corps said: “GOC White Knight Corps visited Ace of Spades Division to review operational preparedness and assess the evolving security dynamics. He was briefed on operational commitments, capability development, UAS & Counter-UAS capabilities and the roadmap ahead.” The Army further said the Corps Commander emphasised enhancing operational effectiveness in an evolving battlefield environment and exhorted all ranks to remain “Future Ready, agile and adaptable” to emerging challenges. The Ace of Spades Division headquartered in the Rajouri-Poonch region is responsible for operational preparedness in a strategically important area along the LoC.

stories.headline: Did we ever count our own 9/11s ?
stories.title: Did we ever count our own 9/11s ?
stories.summary: Twenty-five years after 9/11, when “We Are All Americans” became a universal mantra, there is a pressing need to understand how the faces of terrorism and counter-terrorism have evolved globally. It is worth noting that Jammu and Kashmir experienced its own series of “9/11 moments” both before and after the 2001 attacks in New York. Yet, these repeated atrocities never invoked the same global reaction as the strikes on America. Now, as India takes decisive measures to defend its sovereignty by targeting terrorists and their backers directly across the border, the world is taking cues on how to fight terrorism: by taking the fight straight to the terrorists’ home. Had counter-terrorist operations been conducted with the speed and scale witnessed in recent years, the story of Jammu and Kashmir would have been different.The definition of a 9/11- style attackshould not be judged solely by the catastrophic event. Instead, the true gravity of terrorism needs to be analysed by the lethal intent of the perpetrators and their sponsors. It is precisely through this lens that Jammu and Kashmir reveals a long-standingsystemic pattern of such existential threats. Consequently, any discourse on global terrorism remains fundamentally incomplete without bringing Jammu and Kashmir into the frame. In the months following the 2001 attacks, the then-Chief Minister Farooq Abdullah, frequently shared a telling anecdote. His domestic help rushed into the living room, breathless, where Abdullah was seated with an American guest. The helper urged them to turn on the television, which was broadcasting live, horrific images of planes striking the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York. As the terror unfolded on screen, the American guest huddled in his armchair, paralyzed with fear, his face turning pale. The helper turned to Abdullah and asked in Kashmiri, “What has happened to the guest?” Abdullah replied: “They are witnessing terrorism for the first time—something we experience every single day. We kept telling them that terrorism hits us daily, but the Americans never paid attention. They could never truly understand the pain and horror we were going through. To this day, the deep pain of Kashmir remains misunderstood. Those who supported the Pakistan-sponsored terror project of “Azadi”—or in realistic terms, the violent separation of Kashmir from India—dismissed this suffering as a mere façade. A single brush painted the entire region. Observers failed to see the difference between actual terrorists, their support network, and ordinary citizens. Common people were caught in a violent crossfire, and that was never their choice. The September 11 attacks in America were viewed in stark black and white. The victims were not terrorist sympathizers, nor did an extensive local terror ecosystem exist there on the scale that took decades to build in Kashmir—a reality of bomb explosions, shootings, blood, and rows of lifeless bodies. Jammu and Kashmir witnessed this horrific scale of violence both before and after 9/11. We must understand where these tragedies and their true impact stand. Just weeks after the massive terror attack in America, terrorists targeted the J&K Assembly complex in Srinagar on October 1, 2001. Security forces foiled the takeover, but an explosive-laden vehicle and gunfire killed more than 30 people, including young college girls. This was a massive terror attack—truly the 9/11 of Kashmir. Yet unlike the aftermath in America, there was no global outrage and no talk of retaliation. That time L K Advani was Home Minister. America was busy with its planning to exact retribution from Al-Qaeda and Taliban, responsible for the terror attack with the active technical and material support from Pakistan’s ISI.The top leaders of the two – Osama bin Laden and Mullah Umar were found in Pakistan. Laden neutralized, and Mullah Umar died in a Karachi hospital. India witnessed yet another terror attack – December 13, 2001, when terrorists attempted to storm into theParliament in New Delhi. Amidst this upheaval, India witnessed yet another brazen assault on December 13, 2001, when terrorists attempted to storm the Parliament in New Delhi. The events of 9/11 fundamentally altered the landscape of global terrorism, and Kashmir was no exception. The Hurriyat leadership, which had previously shied away from condemning terrorism, abruptly awoke to this new global reality. Terrorism had finally assumed a definitive shape and narrative that was long overdue, driven by a shifted American attitude that fundamentally altered the discourse. Yet, there was a profound failure on the part of New Delhi’s central leadership, which seemed incapable of deciding on a clear policy to neutralize the threat. An all-out mobilization of troops to the borders yielded only a matching response from the Pakistani side, creating a volatile, war-at-any-moment scenario. Ultimately, it was the shuttle diplomacy of US and Western leaders that defused the situation. India’s so-called “coercive diplomacy” yielded nothing. By this time, a belief had entrenched itself in the Indian psyche—later reinforced by the 26/11 Mumbai attacks—that the country’s leadership lacked an effective counter-terrorism policy, or at least one that matched public expectations. While domestic terrorists were traced and neutralized, and top-notch measures were operationalized to curb infiltration across the Line of Control (LoC), a self-imposed red line remained: do not cross the border. The prevailing logic noted that while Sri Lanka and Pakistan routinely used aerial bombings on terror hideouts, India refrained from doing so. This thesis was premised on two flawed ideas: first, that India should avoid severe measures because a parallel attempt was underway to bring terrorists and their ecosystem to the negotiating table; and second, that India had to remain overly cautious about its international image, as if crossing borders were morally and politically corrosive. This was a misplaced and bizarre line of thought—driven by the fear that the world would be annoyed if Pakistan were hit for harbouring anti-India terrorists, and an inherent anxiety that domestic factions might rise against such actions. This passive approach was amplified not just once, but on several occasions. It raised a host of critical questions about whether Indian citizens were truly safe under a doctrine of self-restraint—a restraint that actively prevented actions that could have changed the course of counter-terrorism. At best, this was a hazy perception of our own making, a myth that desperately needed to be shattered. The Modi government changed the course. By launching the surgical strikes of September 2016 in retribution for the Uri attack; executing aerial strikes against a terror training Centre in Balakot, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, deep inside Pakistan to avenge the February 2019 Pulwama massacre; and finally executing Operation Sindoor in May 2025 to avenge the Pahalgam massacre, New Delhi arun has established an entirely new doctrine for responding to cross-border terrorism.

stories.headline: India rejects IWT court ruling
stories.title: India rejects IWT court ruling
stories.summary: New Delhi, Aug 31: India on Monday rejected the Permanent Court of Arbitration's order setting aside its decision to suspend the Indus Waters Treaty with Pakistan, saying the "illegally-constituted" body has no jurisdiction to comment on New Delhi's sovereign decisions. The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said India's decision to hold the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in abeyance remains in force. New Delhi decided to put the IWT in abeyance as part of a series of punitive diplomatic and economic measures unveiled soon after the Pahalgam terror attack in April last year that killed 26 civilians. Pakistan had approached the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in March this year to determine the status of the treaty virtually challenging India's action. "Today, the illegally constituted so-called Court of Arbitration (CoA) has issued what it termed as an award concerning Interim Measures and Status of the Indus Waters Treaty," the MEA said. "This so called Court was constituted by the World Bank in patent breach of the terms of the Treaty and India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body," it said. India has never recognised the "existence in law of this illegally-constituted and so-called Court of Arbitration", and has always said the "very establishment of this alleged arbitral body constitutes a grave violation of the Indus Waters Treaty", the MEA said in a statement. "Accordingly, India has never appeared before this body and has refused to take any cognisance of its earlier pronouncements," it said. The MEA said the Court of Arbitration has "no jurisdiction whatsoever to pronounce on India's sovereign decisions." "Its pronouncements, now or in the future, will have no effect on India's actions in connection with the projects being undertaken by India," it said. In the last few months, India has stepped up work on several hydropower projects in Jammu and Kashmir that Pakistan had opposed under the provisions of the pact signed in 1960. The Permanent Court of Arbitration said the court considered the meaning of India's decision to suspend the treaty, "finding that it could only be a claim that the Indus Waters Treaty is either suspended or terminated". The court examined the potential grounds on which India can suspend or terminate the Treaty, including grounds cited by New Delhi in its public statements. "In a unanimous decision, the court found that none of these grounds could justify suspension or termination of the Treaty. Accordingly, the Indus Waters Treaty remains fully in force, and India must observe its obligations under the Treaty, including those relating to the design and operation of its hydro-electric projects on the Western Rivers," the Permanent Court of Arbitration said in a media statement. New Delhi has been maintaining that IWT will continue to be held in abeyance until Pakistan "credibly and irrevocably abjures its support for cross-border terrorism". The court said that while India did not participate by making written or oral submissions during proceedings, it took into account India's positions on the issues to the extent "they could be discerned from India's statements and conduct outside of these proceedings (including Indian government communications to Pakistan and to the neutral expert, and public statements made by Indian officials)". The court noted that it looked "extremely seriously" into India's allegation that "Pakistan's sponsorship of cross-border terrorism had impeded its utilisation of rights" under the Indus Waters Treaty. "However, the court found that even if India's allegation was assumed to be true, they would not establish a material breach of the Treaty by Pakistan," the court said. It said the treaty "does not address terrorism or the use of force and expressly indicates that it governs only the rights and obligations of the Parties with respect to the use of the waters of the Indus Rivers System".

stories.headline: CUK receives National HIFFA award
stories.title: CUK receives National HIFFA award
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 31: Head, Department of Mathematics, Central University of Kashmir, Dr. Haribhau R. Bhapkar, has been conferred with the National HIFFA Award for excellence in performance for social transformation through the amalgamation of Mathematics and design thinking. The award was presented by Gulam Ali Khatana, Member of Parliament, and Raja Nighat Aman, SSP Srinagar, at SKICC here Sunday during the 3rd Edition of HIFAA. Jagdambika Pal, Member of Parliament (MP) and the former Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh., inaugurated the award ceremony. Prof. Bhapkar’s recognition comes in appreciation of his multidisciplinary academic contributions and his philosophy of “Mathematics for Social Transformation”, through which he seeks to take mathematics beyond textbooks and apply it to real-world societal challenges. During COVID-19 pandemic, Prof. Bhapkar applied mathematical and design-thinking approaches to conventional methods of measuring pandemic severity. He proposed Progressive Recovery Rate (PRR) and Progressive Mortality Rate (PMR) by incorporating the average recovery time period into pandemic measurement. His research was published in the Journal of Medical Systems, and the work received three copyrights from the Government of India, according to Prof. Bhapkar. During the pandemic, he also provided mathematical analyses through television media and supported the Maharashtra Health Minister. He subsequently presented his work before the Union Minister of State for Health and Family Welfare, and scientists associated with ICMR. Prof. Bhapkar has contributed 100+ research articles, 100+ IPRs and 100+ books authored or co-authored, reflecting the breadth of his academic and research engagement. Prof. Bhapkar is currently working on a ₹1 crore ICSSR project titled “AI and Future of Work”, aimed at preparing marginalised communities for emerging employment opportunities in an increasingly technology-driven economy. Vice Chancellor, Prof. A. Ravinder Nath, congratulated Dr. Bhapkar on receiving the award and said the recognition was a testament to his exceptional academic and research contributions. “Using mathematics as an instrument for social transformation is both innovative and inspiring, and his recognition at the national level brings distinction to CUKashmir,” he said. Dean Academic Affairs, Prof. Shahid Rasool, described the award as a well-deserved recognition of Prof. Bhapkar’s multidisciplinary academic vision and research excellence. Registrar, Dr. Nisar Ahmad Mir, lauded Prof. Bhapkar for his research accomplishments and his sustained efforts to translate mathematical knowledge into solutions for real-world challenges. Dean, School of Physical and Chemical Sciences, Dr. Chandrikalayam Naseema, said that Dr. Bhapkar’s achievement was a matter of pride for the School and the University.

stories.headline: The Mehdi–Abdullah Rupture
stories.title: The Mehdi–Abdullah Rupture
stories.summary: There is a particular cruelty in watching a political marriage end in public, especially when both parties insist the other has broken faith with something larger than themselves. That is the spectacle Jammu and Kashmir has been offered this August, as Srinagar’s Lok Sabha member Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi and National Conference president Dr Farooq Abdullah traded accusations that go well beyond personal pique. Mehdi has now announced he will resign his seat on 3 November, the anniversary of his father’s assassination. Abdullah, for his part, has told him to go and test his standing with the electorate, warning him darkly to remember what happened to the “14 people” who once conspired against his own government in 1984. Beneath the theatre lies a genuine and consequential argument about what the National Conference’s 2024 mandate actually meant, and about whether a party can keep its soul while running a government inside a diminished constitutional shell. A QUARREL WITH A LONG FUSE It is tempting to read this as a sudden combustion, but the rift has been smouldering for nearly two years. Mehdi joined a student agitation over reservation policy as early as December 2024, after which he says the party leadership effectively stopped speaking to him. Through 2025 he pressed, in public and at party forums, for the National Conference to treat restoration of Articles 370 and 35A as a live commitment rather than a rhetorical inheritance, walking out of a working-committee meeting in May after a sharp exchange with Chief Minister Omar Abdullah. By December he was warning of a sit-in over reservation rationalisation and questioning what he called selective demolitions in Jammu. The party’s defeat in the Budgam Assembly bypoll this year appears to have hardened positions on both sides, removing whatever incentive existed for a patched-up truce. What has changed in August 2026 is not the substance of the disagreement but its openness — Farooq Abdullah’s decision to publicly demand resignation, and Mehdi’s decision to answer with a letter rather than a retreat. THE LETTER AS INDICTMENT, NOT APOLOGY Mehdi’s letter to Abdullah is worth reading closely because it refuses the terms on which such letters are usually written. It does not apologise; it interrogates. He notes that Abdullah’s own press remarks — asking Kashmiris how long they would remain “slaves” and accusing critics of “begging” from Delhi — could as easily describe the NC’s own current posture of settling for statehood. His central claim is that statehood was never meant to be a ceiling, only a floor, and that treating it as the outer horizon of political ambition quietly legitimises the constitutional rupture of August 2019. He is not wrong that the 2024 manifesto committed the party to seeking restoration of Articles 370 and 35A alongside statehood; that promise is on paper, not merely in memory. His sharpest line is also his fairest one: the BJP was in power when the manifesto was written, so the argument that restoration is now impossible cannot explain why the promise was made in the first place. ABDULLAH’S CASE, AND ITS LIMITS Dr. Farooq Abdullah’s public response has been blunter than persuasive. Telling Mehdi that his 2024 victory depended on the party symbol, daring him to resign and “go back to the people,” and advising him to consult the Quran to find the “right path” reads less like an argument about strategy and more like an assertion of patriarchal authority. The invocation of 1984 — a year that still carries the scar tissue of Farooq Abdullah’s own government being toppled by defectors — was presumably meant as a warning, but it also inadvertently reveals how personally the NC president has taken this challenge, sixty years into a political life built on exactly the kind of loyalty he now finds wanting in a man he brought into the party himself. What Abdullah has not offered, and what the moment badly needs, is a reasoned defence of sequencing: why statehood first, why Article 370 later, and on what timeline restoration might still be attempted through Parliament rather than through street politics. His single concession — that Mehdi is “a Parliament member” and free to raise Article 370 there — concedes the legitimacy of the demand while declining to own it as party policy. THE DEEPER PROBLEM IS STRUCTURAL, NOT PERSONAL This is where a measured reading must part from both camps. The National Conference’s 2024 manifesto tried to do two things that Kashmir’s current constitutional position makes very difficult to hold together: promise a maximal restoration of pre-2019 status, and promise workable, negotiated governance within a Union Territory administration that reports substantially to Delhi. Those two commitments can coexist as aspirations. They become unstable the moment a party actually forms a government, because governing requires daily transactions with the same authority whose 2019 actions the manifesto pledged to reverse. Mehdi’s insistence on keeping the maximal demand alive is not merely idealism; it names a real risk, that the passage of time converts an emergency into a routine, and that a population’s disempowerment becomes something to be managed rather than resisted. But Abdullah’s insistence on statehood as the practical, sequenced first step also names something real: that a party without administrative power to protect land, jobs, and local institutions cannot fight for anything at all, however loudly it speaks in opposition. WHAT MEHDI’S EXIT WILL AND WILL NOT SETTLE If Mehdi does resign on 3 November as indicated, the ensuing Srinagar by-election will function as an informal referendum, though an imperfect one, on whether his position commands an independent electoral base or was always borrowed from the National Conference’s organisational strength. Abdullah has bet, publicly and repeatedly, that Mehdi’s 2024 margin of over 350,000 votes belonged to the party symbol, not the man. Mehdi has bet that his own credibility — as the son of a man killed for his politics, and as a rare voice within a ruling party willing to embarrass his own chief minister — will translate into votes cast on principle. Both men are, in effect, gambling with the same electorate’s patience. Whatever the by-election shows, it will not resolve the structural tension that produced this rupture. Even if Mehdi wins as an independent—or loses and recedes from immediate political prominence—the National Conference will still be governing a Union Territory after having promised a wider constitutional restoration that it has yet to deliver. The next MP from Srinagar, whoever it may be, will inherit the same unresolved question Mehdi’s letter has placed before Farooq Abdullah: has the party’s political horizon permanently narrowed to what New Delhi is willing to concede, or does its 2024 promise still carry political meaning? That question will outlast this particular feud and, in all likelihood, the present protagonists. The National Conference’s future will not be decided by a quarrel between personalities, nor by whether Mehdi ultimately returns to its fold. It will be decided by whether the party still believes that its promises are obligations rather than instruments of electoral convenience. If a party that sought votes in the name of constitutional dignity now treats that very promise as a negotiable inconvenience, it may retain the seat of government while losing the confidence that once made it a movement. The real test, therefore, is not only what Mehdi will do next. It is whether the National Conference can recover the moral courage to clarify its course, renew its pledge, and keep faith with those who voted for it. Until it does, the Valley’s political future will remain unsettled—not because dissent has weakened the party, but because the party has yet to answer the dissent that its own promises have produced. While in service, he also served as the UN Liaison Officer across 42 countries with Iraq’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Baghdad after the First Gulf War.

stories.headline: Rivers, Electricity, and Bills
stories.title: Rivers, Electricity, and Bills
stories.summary: There is something deeply uncomfortable about another electricity tariff hike in Jammu and Kashmir. This is a place where rivers tumble down from the mountains, ambitious hydropower projects are being built and electricity has long been presented as one of J&K’s greatest natural advantages. Yet the story reaching the ordinary consumer remains familiar that the power sector runs on deficit, the government provides support and the consumer is asked to pay more. From 1st September 2026, electricity tariffs in J&K are set to rise by an average 6.83 percent. For 2026-27, the revenue requirement of JPDCL and KPDCL has been assessed at roughly ₹10,276 crore against revenue of about ₹7,353 crore at existing tariffs, leaving a gap of approximately ₹2,923 crore. The government has committed around ₹2,421 crore in support, leaving roughly ₹502 crore to be recovered through the tariff revision. Had the entire deficit been passed on to consumers, the increase could have approached 40 percent. While the subsidy reduces the immediate burden on consumers, it does not address the underlying financial weaknesses of the power sector or explain why consumers should continue to bear the cost of a system that remains structurally inefficient. But it cannot be the end of the debate. A tariff hike can raise revenue. It cannot by itself repair a financially weak distribution system, eliminate power theft, reduce technical losses, improve collection or make expensive power procurement cheaper. If these problems continue, today’s tariff increase will only postpone tomorrow’s deficit. The real question is therefore simple that what will consumers get in return for paying more? Government support to JPDCL and KPDCL should increasingly be linked to measurable performance including lower distribution losses, better collection efficiency, greater reliability and more efficient procurement. Smart meters and feeder level monitoring should produce measurable results, not merely installation figures. Every rupee of public support should either make the system more efficient or protect the consumer more effectively. This becomes particularly important when we revisit the promise of 200 free units. During the 2024 Assembly election campaign, the government promised 200 units of free electricity for every household, irrespective of social category. After coming to power, however, the promise was narrowed to around 2.23 lakh Antyodaya Anna Yojana families and linked to a rooftop solar scheme. The irony is that this rooftop solar scheme is itself a Central Government initiative. J&K has roughly 20 lakh domestic consumers based on recent available figures. If 20 lakh is taken as a working assumption, 200 units a month valued at ₹2.45 per unit would represent approximately ₹1,176 crore annually. This is only an illustrative calculation, not an official costing because the actual liability would depend on eligibility, consumption and tariff slabs. Even so, the comparison is striking. The present tariff revision is expected to recover around ₹502 crore while the illustrative value of 200 free units for all domestic consumers would be around ₹1,200 crore. This does not mean the government could simply spend ₹1,200 crore and make electricity free. Public finance does not work that way. But it does show that choices exist. The larger question is whether that money should merely bridge an annual gap or whether part of it can protect vulnerable consumers while the rest is tied to reforms that reduce the gap itself. Subsidies have a role, but they should be targeted and transparent rather than becoming a permanent substitute for efficiency. There is another question J&K cannot avoid that what does our hydropower wealth mean for the ordinary electricity consumer? For decades, the people of J&K have been told that despite having enormous hydropower potential, the Union Territory remains energy deficient because many of the major projects are developed and owned by the Central Government or central-sector entities, while J&K’s share of the electricity generated is limited. That may explain part of the structural reality, but it cannot be the end of the conversation. The ordinary consumer has little control over who owns a project, how its power is allocated or how electricity is procured. A family paying its electricity bill cannot be expected to solve an institutional problem created by decades of power-sector arrangements. If J&K does not receive enough of the electricity or economic value generated from projects located within its territory, then the responsibility lies with the government to negotiate better terms, strengthen J&K’s generation capacity, improve its share and make the best possible use of the benefits it does receive. Perhaps it is time to stop telling consumers why J&K is energy deficient and start telling them what the government is doing to change that reality. The common man cannot change the ownership structure of hydropower projects; the government can. The common man cannot renegotiate power-sharing arrangements; the government can. The common man cannot redesign the distribution system; the government must. The burden of fixing this structural imbalance cannot simply be transferred to consumers through higher tariffs. Moreover, it is time to think of hydropower not merely in megawatts but as a public dividend. The comparison with neighbouring states also raises questions about policy choices. While J&K has approved an average 6.83 percent tariff increase for 2026–27, Punjab has reduced domestic tariffs, Himachal Pradesh has marginally reduced energy charges and Haryana has kept tariffs unchanged. The comparison does not erase J&K’s own financial constraints, but it does show that tariff policy is ultimately a matter of choices as well as costs. Further communities that host major hydro power projects should not merely bear the physical and environmental realities of development; they should also share in its economic benefits. This matters especially in District Kishtwar, where the risks are not simply a matter of speculation. The District Disaster Management Authority’s Glacial Lake Outburst Flood Risk Management Plan for 2024–25 records 197 glacial lakes in the district, accounting for 36.08 percent of all glacial lakes in J&K and highlights the vulnerability of the upper Chenab basin to glacial and other mountain hazards. This is the landscape that is giving its rivers and mountains to a massive hydropower push. The people living here are being asked to accept the disruption, the uncertainty and the risks that come with developing such a fragile Himalayan region. After all this sacrifice, what should they reasonably expect in return? Surely not simply another increase in their electricity bills. If Chenab area bears the risks while its rivers generate power for the wider system, then its people must also share meaningfully in the benefits. Development cannot mean that the mountains and communities bear the burden while the benefits flow elsewhere. When people are asked to sacrifice for development but are denied a fair share of its benefits, it ceases to be a question of economics alone. It becomes a question of humanity. Ultimately, this is not a debate about whether electricity should be free or whether consumers should pay. It is a debate about fairness. If our rivers are being harnessed, our mountains are being developed, our communities are carrying the risks and our people are being asked to pay more for electricity, then the people of J&K should not merely inherit the bills; they should inherit a meaningful share of the benefits. The answer cannot be to keep explaining why J&K is energy deficient while asking its people to shoulder more of the burden. The answer must be a power sector that delivers reliable electricity, protects vulnerable consumers and ensures that the wealth generated by our rivers creates lasting value for the people who call these mountains home. A tariff hike can plug a hole. It cannot repair a leaking system. Our rivers should generate more than electricity; they should generate dignity, opportunity and a dividend for the people of J&K. If development demands sacrifice from the people, justice demands that its benefits reach them too. Peerzada Mohsin Shafi hails from Anantnag and writes on infrastructure-related issues.

If our rivers are being harnessed, our mountains are being developed, our communities are carrying the risks and our people are being asked to pay more for electricity, then the people of J&K should not merely inherit the bills; they should inherit a meaningful share of the benefits.
The answer cannot be to keep explaining why J&K is energy deficient while asking its people to shoulder more of the burden.

The answer must be a power sector that delivers reliable electricity, protects vulnerable consumers and ensures that the wealth generated by our rivers creates lasting value for the people who call these mountains home.
A tariff hike can plug a hole.
It cannot repair a leaking system.

Our rivers should generate more than electricity; they should generate dignity, opportunity and a dividend for the people of J&K. If development demands sacrifice from the people, justice demands that its benefits reach them too.
Peerzada Mohsin Shafi hails from Anantnag and writes on infrastructure-related issues.

stories.title: Application of Load Management
stories.summary: The Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission for the Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh (JERC, JKL) has issued a new tariff order for Jammu & Kashmir effective from September 1, 2026. While the order provides for an average increase of 6.83 per cent in retail electricity tariffs for FY 2026-27, it also introduces the Time of Day (ToD) tariff for all categories of consumers except agriculture. The new tariff structure offers consumers an opportunity to reduce their electricity bills by shifting electricity usage to specific hours of the day. Time of Day tariff is a pricing mechanism under which electricity charges vary according to the time at which electricity is consumed. Under the tariff order, ToD charges are applicable in addition to normal energy charges for consumers with a sanctioned load exceeding 10 kW. The Commission has divided the day into three periods: Solar Hours from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM, Peak Hours from 6:00 AM to 9:00 AM and 5:00 PM to 10:00 PM, and Normal Hours from 10:00 PM to 6:00 AM. Consumers are entitled to a 20 per cent rebate on energy charges during Solar Hours, encouraging greater use of electricity when solar power generation is available and energy procurement costs are lower. During Peak Hours, industrial and commercial consumers are required to pay a 20 per cent surcharge on energy charges, while other eligible consumer categories attract a surcharge of 10 per cent. Normal Hours carry neither a surcharge nor a rebate and are billed at standard tariff rates. The financial benefits of the ToD tariff can be substantial. Consider the example of water heating requiring 100 units of electricity at a normal tariff of Rs. 5 per unit. Under standard conditions, the cost would be Rs. 500. If the electricity is consumed during Solar Hours, the 20 per cent rebate reduces the cost to Rs. 400, resulting in a saving of Rs. 100. On the other hand, if the same electricity is consumed during Peak Hours, industrial and commercial consumers would pay Rs. 600 because of the 20 per cent surcharge, while other eligible consumers would pay Rs. 550 due to the 10 per cent surcharge. Thus, by simply shifting this 100-unit load from Peak Hours to Solar Hours, a consumer can reduce the cost from Rs. 600 to Rs. 400, achieving a saving of Rs. 200 or about 33 per cent. This clearly demonstrates how flexible loads such as water heating can be scheduled more economically while making better use of available solar energy. To maximize the benefits of the ToD tariff, consumers will need to adopt effective load management practices. Electricity-intensive activities should be shifted, wherever possible, to Solar Hours between 9:00 AM and 5:00 PM. Single-shift industries, government offices and educational institutions, whose normal operations largely fall within this period, are well positioned to benefit from the 20 per cent rebate without making major operational changes. Hotels and other commercial establishments can similarly reduce costs by operating water-heating systems and other flexible loads during Solar Hours. Non-continuous industrial processes should preferably be avoided during Peak Hours in order to minimize the impact of surcharges. Through such measures, consumers can substantially reduce their electricity expenditure while supporting efficient utilization of available energy resources. The implementation of the ToD tariff, however, presents significant operational challenges for the distribution companies of Jammu & Kashmir, namely Jammu Power Distribution Corporation Limited (JPDCL) and Kashmir Power Distribution Corporation Limited (KPDCL). Effective implementation requires at least six meter readings per month from each consumer, including four readings corresponding to the prescribed ToD slots, cumulative energy consumption and maximum demand. The legacy meters currently in service may be configured for different time-slot structures that do not match the Commission’s newly prescribed schedule. Reprogramming these meters on a large scale is a complex undertaking. In addition, manpower limitations and technical constraints related to meter reading and data management may further complicate implementation. Smart meters, however, provide a practical solution by automatically transmitting detailed consumption data at regular intervals, enabling accurate allocation of electricity usage across the prescribed ToD periods. The ToD tariff has been introduced by the Commission in compliance with the Ministry of Power, Government of India Notification No. G.S.R. 437(E) dated 14 June 2023, issued under the Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Amendment Rules, 2023. The Rules mandated the implementation of Time of Day (ToD) tariff for commercial and industrial consumers having a maximum demand exceeding 10 kW from a date not later than 1 April 2024. For all other consumers, except agricultural consumers, the ToD tariff was required to be implemented not later than 1 April 2025. Further, for consumers equipped with smart meters, the ToD tariff shall become effective immediately upon installation of the smart meter. The broader objective of the ToD tariff extends beyond consumer savings. It is intended to encourage greater electricity consumption during daytime hours when solar power is available in abundance. This is particularly important because the country’s battery storage capacity remains limited compared to its rapidly growing solar generation capacity. Despite an installed solar capacity of about 165 GW, battery storage capacity is only around 5.9 GW, representing approximately 3.5% of the installed solar capacity. By aligning electricity demand with periods of high solar generation, the ToD tariff promotes more effective integration of renewable energy into the power system. Increased utilization of solar energy reduces dependence on conventional thermal generation, lowers greenhouse gas emissions, improves air quality and contributes to climate change mitigation. At the same time, reducing demand during peak periods eases pressure on generation, transmission and distribution infrastructure, leading to improved reliability, operational efficiency and better financial sustainability of electricity utilities. These benefits ultimately serve the interests of both consumers and power companies. For further technical details on the Time of Day tariff, readers may watch the video on the subject available on my YouTube channel, Bashir Dar @ JKGT. Er. stories.headline: Met predicts isolated spell of heavy rains in Jammu division for 2 days
stories.title: Met predicts isolated spell of heavy rains in Jammu division for 2 days
stories.summary: Amid persisting orange alert across Jammu for two days, the weather department has predicted isolated heavy rains with thunder storms, lightning and gusty winds for the entire Jammu region, with the possibilities of landslides, shooting stones and flash floods at vulnerable places on September 1 and 2. During the next 24 hours, as per weatherman, there will be isolated heavy falls in Jammu division while there will be fairly widespread light to moderate rain coupled with thunderstorms in the subsequent two days. As per India Meteorological Department (IMD) Centre, parts of the division may witness spells of showers with gusty winds during late night on Monday, August 31. “In Jammu division, during the intervening nights of August 31-September 1 and September 1 and 2, there is possibility of heavy spell particularly in Jammu, Kathua districts and adjoining areas. Rajouri-Poonch areas too may witness a spell or two of isolated moderate to heavy showers during next 24 to 48 hours,” the weatherman predicted. “There are chances of heavy showers in Jammu division with the possibility of mudslides, landslides and flash floods at higher and vulnerable places. After September 2, there will be improvement in the weather. Till September 10, there are no chances of major events,” the Met department has anticipated. The weather conditions would continue to be hot and humid amid scattered spells. The maximum temperature in Jammu is likely to swing between 31 to 33 degrees Celsius, amid hot and humid weather conditions. After September 15, according to the weatherman, the temperature is likely to witness a significant fall.
